entry.title: Combined summary - [BIP Draft] Co-signer Spending Policies
entry.summary: A new proposal has emerged to standardize co-signer spending policies in Bitcoin, targeting the rules and conditions under which a co-signer may sign a transaction rather than mandating how co-signers themselves operate. This initiative is a response to the fragmented landscape of current co-signed transaction protocols, such as Halseth’s blinded co-signers, Chain Code Delegation, and contemporary products like Liquidium and Lendasat, all of which have developed their own incompatible policy formats. The lack of interoperability among these systems not only complicates integration across wallets and co-signers but also hinders auditability and innovation. By focusing on a universal, portable format for describing what evidence or attestations are required for a co-signer to approve a spend, the proposal aims to provide the foundation for open, auditable, and composable financial protocols. The draft outlines several verification processes including open verification, blinded verification, and enclave verification to ensure that policies governing co-signature are enforced securely and transparently. These processes accommodate both transaction-derived and external attestations, such as those from Discreet Log Contract (DLC) oracles, without requiring changes to the oracles' existing interfaces. The requirement that every script enforceable by Bitcoin Script be explicitly included in the policy ensures that there is always a direct execution path—meaning funds cannot become irretrievably frozen should co-signers disappear. The complete specification, along with ongoing discussions and updates, is available as a [Bitcoin Improvement Proposal](https://github.com/lukecarriere/bip-cosigner-spending-policies/blob/468fdd1b75647432ed56c3a2b5579cbcfedaec74/bip-cosigner-spending-policies.md). A critical component of the policy format is its approach to serialization and semantic commitment. Several candidate formats are considered: TLV (Type-Length-Value), canonical JSON, and deterministic CBOR. TLV, while not human-readable, offers strict field ordering and uniqueness, aligning closely with Lightning Network and DLC standards. Canonical JSON provides readability and ubiquity but introduces risks related to byte-level inconsistencies and duplicate keys unless rigorously controlled. Deterministic CBOR is compact and already used for certain wallet operations, but differences in library implementations could cause interoperability issues. A hybrid model is being considered, where cryptographic commitments and policy IDs are derived strictly from TLV encoding, with a parallel JSON format for authoring and review. This approach seeks to balance the needs for machine-verifiable security and human accessibility, though it increases the burden on specification and testing. Ensuring precise semantic interpretation across implementations is paramount. The policy hash must encode not just syntactic validity but the exact semantics of verification, specifying how unknown fields, duplicates, and default values are treated. Strict validation mandates that any policy containing unknown or duplicate fields is invalid; every field must be serialized explicitly, leaving no room for ambiguity. The policy ID is constructed as a BIP340 tagged hash with the tag `CSP/policy/v0`, ensuring domain separation from statement and transaction hashes. This design guarantees that two independent implementations will agree on the policy ID and the accept-or-reject decision for any given policy document, provided they follow the same explicit rules. The signing process for statements (currently at version 0) involves attesting to an event ID, outcome, and timestamp. However, initial responses may later be updated—particularly in scenarios reliant on human judgment, such as escrow delivery. To address the risk of acting on preliminary rather than final outcomes, a finality flag will be incorporated, allowing attestors to indicate when an outcome is definitive. Policies can require this confirmation before allowing a co-signature, or else specify a dispute window if finality is never declared. In the context of DLCs utilizing nonce pre-commitment, protocol-level safeguards ensure that signing conflicting outcomes exposes the attestor’s key, providing strong guarantees against equivocation. Test vectors for policy IDs and signed statements will accompany the chosen serialization format to underpin cross-platform consistency. The proposal’s vision extends well beyond lending. It defines seven foundational components for a robust, open lending protocol capable of replacing centralized, rehypothecating lenders like Celsius and BlockFi. Each loan remains one-to-one and non-custodial, with borrowers retaining control of their collateral via standard PSBTs and descriptors. Offers are negotiated openly, price feeds and payment proofs come from signed DLC oracle data, and the co-signer releases or liquidates collateral strictly according to the standardized policy. An alert service notifies parties of margin calls without possessing funds, and agreement templates tie exact terms to policy IDs for transparency and automation. If broadly adopted, this standard unlocks portability across lenders, fosters competition and composability, and removes single points of failure. Auditability is enhanced, enabling anyone to verify policy rules before engaging in financial contracts.
